title: Forked children preserve the parent request prefix
summary: A forked child agent keeps the same tool list and system prompt prefix as its parent and receives its task after the inherited history, so the provider can reuse the cached request prefix.
firstReason: Prefix reuse is the whole payoff of fork over spawn; keep the byte-identical prefix rule.

title: Adjacent Agents share one Steer send_message operation
summary: Parent and child agents use one send_message operation in both directions; it always delivers by steering the target and records one durable source that names the sender.
firstReason: One operation for messages between adjacent agents replaces two direction-specific tools and schemas; keep it.

title: Parent-owned subagent catalog events
summary: The parent session records each direct child agent in its own durable catalog events, which are the authority for finding children; nothing scans all sessions or opens child logs to discover them.
firstReason: The creator already knows the fact, so recording it where it is created keeps discovery cost independent of the number of sessions; keep it.

title: Subagent identity in required runtime context
summary: A subagent's identity (its own, its parent's and its root's session id) is supplied as required runtime context derived from the live subagent tree, not written into its first task message.
firstReason: Identity in the first message can be removed by compaction and is wrong after a fork. Deriving it from the live tree at each request keeps it current. This is agent-loop behaviour and language-neutral.

title: Agent Teams teammates are subagents
summary: A team member is an ordinary subagent identified by its session id; there is no separate team roster and there are no member names. Every root agent and its descendants form the team, and the team feature adds only task tools and task policy.
firstReason: A second roster duplicated identity, recovery and teardown, and forced profiles to disable ordinary delegation. One identity model is simpler to build in Go from the start.

title: Communication follows the subagent tree
summary: Listing agents and sending messages work across the whole subagent tree under one root, not only between parent and child. The sender must be a live member of the same tree, and delivery re-checks that at final admission.
firstReason: A team shares one task board across the tree, so adjacent-only messaging forced relays through parents. Authorization by tree membership with a final re-check is the rule to carry.

title: Team task boards share ordinary subagent waits
summary: The team feature owns only task storage, dependencies and compare-and-set task commands. Identity, discovery, messaging, interruption and waiting come from the ordinary subagent tools, and task state is read from the task journal, not delivered as messages.
firstReason: It removes a second roster and a second wake-up channel. Fewer overlapping mechanisms is a direct simplification for the Go build.

title: Team availability is selected per Session
summary: Team mode is a saved choice on the root session, default off, made in the model menu; it is not a plugin switch in the shared profile. Turning it off keeps the task journal and the child agents.
firstReason: A profile-level switch changed other sessions and needed a config edit to try collaboration once. Per-session selection is product behaviour.

title: User controls address the target subagent
summary: A browser prompt or a user interruption for a subagent addresses only that child session, and each method declares that session as its access resource. Access to a parent or to the global resource does not imply access to the child.
firstReason: A caller-supplied parent id proved consistency, not identity or permission. Per-target authorization follows from the principal model in the remote-access note.

title: Subagent tools own communication guidance
summary: The subagent messaging tool plugin owns the guidance about how and when a child reports to its parent, emitted as runtime context only when its tool is actually available. The continuation manager owns result delivery.
firstReason: The manager used to detect one tool implementation through a hidden marker. Guidance that travels with the tool that needs it is the same composition rule as the preset-scoped notes.

title: Subagent names live in the creator's catalog
summary: Each child agent gets a short name (1 to 32 lower-case letters, digits or hyphens, default `agent-N`) that is unique among its creator's children and stored in the creator's catalog entry. The session id stays the only execution identity; a name is a model-facing reference that tools resolve to it.
firstReason: Models copy 36-character ids badly and pay tokens for them in every listing; a short name fixes a model-facing problem that does not depend on the host language. The synchronous reservation at admission maps to a mutex-guarded set in Go.

title: Subagent end-turn guidance stays in the delegation paragraph
summary: The delegation guidance keeps the sentence that tells the model to end its turn when only waiting for subagent results remains, instead of sleeping or polling; a settled child delivers a notice that starts a new turn.
firstReason: The sentence was measured upstream to stop long sleep loops (about 25 minutes of sleeping in one recorded session). Prompt text is model-facing and carries over; the remark about re-rendering prompt snapshot files is upstream repository mechanics.

title: Shared preset delegation tools
summary: Each delegation tool instance registers its definition once, in the composition that owns it, and agents sharing a preset revision inherit it. A preset switch changes ancestry and needs no per-agent installation, and the tool schema lists preset ids without the candidates' descriptions.
firstReason: Per-agent installation left a window in which the tools were missing and put them in a layer exempt from inherited restrictions. Inheritance through the context tree is how the Go cordis port scopes registrations.

title: Configure subagent persona, tool visibility, and depth
summary: `maxDepth` is an absolute cap on how deep a delegation tree may grow, and a provider declares whether it can enforce it. Persona and tool-filter overrides are no longer accepted for new children (presets own composition) and survive only to restore children recorded in old sessions.
firstReason: The depth cap is a safety bound worth keeping. The persona and tool-filter restore paths exist only to read historical upstream sessions, which DH-ADR-2 says the Go design need not do, so only the depth policy carries over.

title: Continuable subagents
summary: A continuable subagent is one durable session with at most one live Activation (one period in which its reconstructed agent is resident in the process). The agent's own inbox is the only turn queue; an Activation may run several turns and stay resident while waiting for descendants, and its receipt owns the result and cancellation of that one residency.
firstReason: Separating the durable conversation from the process-local residency removes a second queue and the coupling of background-task lifetime to conversation delivery. The model is about ownership and is language-neutral.

title: Durable Agent Teams over continuable children
summary: Every root session and its descendants form a Team identified by the root session id, with a durable compare-and-set task board. One package owns the durable semantics (`ctx.agentTeams`) and another the model-facing tools, whose results are compact JSON with declared schemas.
firstReason: Peer addressing and a shared task board with protection against stale updates are needed for multi-agent work in any implementation.

title: Product subagents use Profile-selected non-interactive permissions
summary: The Claude Code and Codex subagent providers run unattended with a `permissionMode` fixed in the deployment profile, using each product's own mode names. The subagent tool schema carries no permission field, so a model or a single delegation cannot raise its own authority.
firstReason: Authority fixed by the operator and unreachable from the model is the point, and it is language-neutral. The Claude Code provider upstream uses an npm SDK; the Go provider has to drive the product another way, which the subagent area decides.

title: User-authorized subagent model routes
summary: A host setting stores an `enabled` switch and an explicit list of exact `{ provider, model }` routes that a parent agent may choose for a child. Registering a new model adapter never widens the list, and each delegation call reads the current setting.
firstReason: Explicit, stable authorization of model routes prevents a silent growth of cost and capability when a provider or model appears.

title: Independent spawn preset selection and restoration
summary: An explicit spawn preset resolves the currently registered definition; omitting it joins the parent's exact live composition. On restore, an independent selection is recognized by an `agent-preset/selected` event recorded before the child's first descriptor, a marker chosen so that the session format did not have to change.
firstReason: The selection and inheritance semantics stand. The ordering marker exists only to stay compatible with historical logs; the Go session format can record the selection as an explicit field when the child is created.

title: Interactive side sessions and merge-back
summary: Proposal, not built upstream: a side session is an ordinary live session forked at the source's last completed turn and framed as a read-only advisor, which the user talks to separately and which can merge one condensed note back into the parent.
firstReason: Adopt as deferred scope. It composes primitives the Go design already keeps (session fork, agent attach, injected context) and needs no new mechanism, but upstream has not built or validated it, so it should not be in the first stages.

title: Live subagent model-selection setting
summary: The list of models a subagent may be routed to is read from the live setting at each call, instead of being copied into each session when it is created. A change to the setting applies to the next call in every running, restored and child session.
firstReason: A setting that takes effect immediately is easier to explain than one whose meaning depends on when a session was created. The Go design keeps the live read and, because it does not read upstream session logs (DH-ADR-2), does not need the retired session event upstream still declares.

title: Unified subagent activations
summary: Every way of running a subagent goes through one entry point that returns a handle with the child's identity, a result that settles only after cleanup, and disposal of exactly that activation. Local providers only contribute preparation data; the subagent service owns agent creation and lifetime.
firstReason: One owner for creation, cancellation, result and cleanup removes the separate paths that used to disagree. In Go the handle maps onto a value with a context for cancellation and a result that is delivered after cleanup.

title: Preset-owned subagent composition
summary: A subagent's persona and tool set come from the Agent Preset it selects, not from separate persona and tool-filter settings on the subagent tool. The removed settings are rejected at load instead of being silently ignored.
firstReason: One place to compose an agent is easier to reason about than two. The Go design keeps preset-owned composition and the rule that an unknown configuration key is an error; it does not need the parsing upstream retains for child descriptors written by older releases (DH-ADR-2).

title: Inbox-only Agent waits
summary: The `wait_agent` tool ends only when a message arrives in its caller's own inbox (or on timeout or cancellation). Task-board edits and other agents' activity do not wake it; a caller who wants a team member to act sends an explicit message.
firstReason: A wait that ends without a message leaves the model with nothing to act on. The narrower rule also keeps team coordination out of ordinary subagent controls, and maps directly onto a Go channel or subscription on one inbox.

title: Team projection retains only tasks and mode
summary: The team state derived from the session log holds only the task list and the saved mode. Older member and mailbox records are ignored instead of being replayed through retired validators that could fail the current task board.
firstReason: The Go team projection should contain only tasks and mode from the start. The other half of the note, ignoring historical member and message records, has nothing to ignore in Go because upstream session logs are not read (DH-ADR-2).
